title: Key Lemma: n ≡ 3 (mod 4) Has a Prime Factor ≡ 3 (mod 4)
content: The core lemma: any $n > 1$ with $n \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ has a prime factor $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. The proof uses well-founded recursion (`termination_by n`). Take any prime factor $p$ of $n$. If $p \equiv 3$, done. Otherwise, since $n$ is odd ($n \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$), we have $p \neq 2$, so $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. Writing $n = pk$, we get $k \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ (since $1 \cdot k \equiv 3$), $k > 1$, and $k < n$ (since $p \geq 2$). By the induction hypothesis, $k$ has a prime factor $q \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, which also divides $n$.
mathContext:
$n > 1,\; n \equiv 3 \pmod{4} \implies \exists p \mid n,\; p \text{ prime},\; p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.
Contrapositive: a product of primes $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ is $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$.

title: Multiplicativity of Residues mod 4
content: The hidden engine of the proof: the group $(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})^\times = \{1, 3\}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Since $1 \cdot 1 = 1$, $1 \cdot 3 = 3$, and $3 \cdot 3 = 1$ modulo 4, the product of numbers $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ stays $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. So a number $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ must have an odd number of prime factors $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. The proof extracts this using `Nat.mul_mod` and the hypothesis `hpmod1 : p % 4 = 1`.
mathContext: $(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})^\times \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$: products of residues $\equiv 1$ stay $\equiv 1$; an odd count of $\equiv 3$ gives $\equiv 3$.

title: Euclid-Style Construction: N = 4(n+1)! - 1
content: Given any bound $n$, the construction $N = 4(n+1)! - 1$ is a careful variant of Euclid's proof of infinite primes. The number $N$ satisfies three properties simultaneously: (1) $N \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ since $4(n+1)! \equiv 0 \pmod{4}$ and subtracting 1 gives $\equiv 3$; (2) $N > 1$ since $(n+1)! \geq 1$; (3) any prime factor $p \leq n+1$ divides $(n+1)!$ and hence $4(n+1)! = N+1$, but not $N$ (since $\gcd(N, N+1) = 1$). The use of `Set.infinite_iff_exists_gt` converts the infinitude statement to: for every $n$, there exists a prime $p > n$ with $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.
mathContext:
$N = 4(n+1)! - 1 \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, $N > 1$.
If $p \leq n+1$: $p \mid (n+1)! \mid N+1$, so $p \nmid N$ (since $\gcd(N, N+1) = 1$).

title: Bounding the Prime Factor: p > n via Contradiction
content: The proof that $p > n$ proceeds by contradiction: assume $p \leq n$, then $p \leq n+1$, so $p \mid (n+1)!$ by `Nat.Prime.dvd_factorial`. Since $N + 1 = 4(n+1)!$, we get $p \mid N+1$. Combined with $p \mid N$, this gives $p \mid (N+1) - N = 1$, so $p \leq 1$, contradicting $p \geq 2$ (primality). The Lean proof uses `nlinarith` with the equations $N = pa$ and $N+1 = pb$ to derive $p(b-a) = 1$, forcing $p \leq 1$.
mathContext: $p \mid N \land p \mid (N+1) \implies p \mid 1 \implies p \leq 1$, contradicting $p$ prime.

title: Existence Witness: 3 is Prime and ≡ 3 (mod 4)
content: A simple witness establishing that the set of primes $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ is nonempty: $3$ is prime and $3 \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. Both facts are discharged by `norm_num`. While the main theorem already implies nonemptiness (via infinitude), this explicit witness is useful for computations and as a base case.
